title: Joshua 5:13–15
context: Joshua 5:13–15 describes Joshua meeting a man with a drawn sword near Jericho. Asked whose side he is on, he answers that he has come as commander of the LORD’s army. Joshua falls down and worships, and he is told to take off his sandals because the ground is holy, an echo of Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5). Interpreters differ on the commander’s identity. Many read him as a theophany or as the angel of the LORD, and others as a high-ranking created angel. That question cuts across both traditions rather than dividing them. Both agree the scene teaches that the battle belongs to the LORD and that Joshua’s first duty is reverence.

verses.text: When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man stood in front of him with his sword drawn in his hand. Joshua went to him and said to him, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?”
verses.arminianNotes: Near Jericho, Joshua sees a man with a drawn sword and asks whether he is for Israel or for its enemies. Arminian readers note that Joshua frames the question in terms of sides, the natural concern of a commander, and the scene prepares him to learn that the real question is whether he stands on the LORD’s side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The drawn sword recalls the angel of the LORD with drawn sword before Balaam (Numbers 22:31) and before David (1 Chronicles 21:16). Both traditions see a heavenly visitor revealed to Joshua at the threshold of the campaign, before any human strategy is formed.

verses.text: He said, “No; but I have come now as commander of the LORD’s army.” Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, “What does my lord say to his servant?”
verses.arminianNotes: He answers "No," saying he has come as commander of the LORD’s army, and Joshua falls down and worships. Arminians read the answer as a correction: God is not a tool for Israel’s side, and Israel must align with God. Some in the tradition read the figure as the angel of the LORD or a preincarnate appearance of the Son, while others read him as a created angel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the answer puts Joshua under God’s command. Many Reformed writers read the commander as a theophany or the angel of the LORD, partly because he receives Joshua’s worship and calls the ground holy, while others hold that he is a high created angel. Neither tradition settles the identity with certainty, and the view is not a dividing line between them.

verses.text: The prince of the LORD’s army said to Joshua, “Take off your sandals, for the place on which you stand is holy.” Joshua did so.
verses.arminianNotes: The prince of the LORD’s army tells Joshua to take off his sandals because the place is holy, and Joshua obeys. Arminians see the deliberate echo of Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5), confirming that the God of Moses is with Joshua as he promised (Joshua 1:5).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the encounter ends with Joshua’s obedience rather than battle orders. Many connect this scene with the instructions for Jericho that follow in 6:2–5. Both traditions see holiness and worship coming before conquest, with Joshua as a servant before he is a general.
